The 6-km-wide Tsirk caldera formed during the Pleistocene. The caldera floor contains a hot lake (Gorshkov 1970).

Kuntomintar is a Pleistocene andesitic stratovolcano at the southern end of Shiashkotan Island in the central Kuriles. A central cone fills a 4-4.5 km caldera, whose rim is visible on the NE side. A second caldera on the west side is breached to the west.

Shestakov is an eroded volcanic complex in the north-central part of Onekotan Island, south of the Nemo Peak caldera system. Gorshkov (1970) notes that this "massif was formed in preglacial times and then underwent glacial abrasion and postglacial erosion to such a degree that at present it is extremely difficult to re…

The small basaltic Mashkovtsev stratovolcano forms a peninsula on the Sea of Okhotsk near the southern tip of the Kamchatka Peninsula. It was considered Holocene by Masurenkov (1980), and there is a postglacial summit cone (Sviatlovsky 1959). Two basaltic cones are located to the north.

Kell volcano is a small stratovolcano considered to be Holocene by Masurenkov (1980), located within the Prizrak caldera immediately north of Zheltovsky volcano. This remote volcanic complex consists of three partially nested 3-5 km wide calderas containing lava domes and several small stratovolcanoes, the largest of w…

Belenkaya is a small basaltic volcano considered to be Holocene by Masurenkov (1980) that lies SW of Ksudach and NW of Kell. The conical stratovolcano rises 700 m above a topographic low in the center of the southern Kamchatka Peninsula. This was not included by Ponomareva et al.

Piratkovsky, identified by Masurenkov (1980) as a mid-Pleistocene to Holocene stratovolcano with a small caldera, is NE of Khodutka volcano. It partially overlaps Pleistocene volcanoes to the NW and lies at the eastern margin of the Quaternary volcanic chain of southern Kamchatka.

The Ostanets shield volcano, considered to be Holocene by Masurenkov (1980), is located south of the Pleistocene Savan volcano surrounded by a large group of late-Pleistocene to Holocene cinder cones. Small pyroclastic cone groups also occur north and east of Igolki volcano, ~30 km SW of Savan.

The Otdelniy shield volcano, considered early Holocene by Masurenkov (1980), lies east of the Savan River, across from the Pleistocene Savan volcano. It, along with adjacent shield volcanoes and a large group of late-Pleistocene to Holocene basaltic pyroclastic cones, is about halfway between Khodutka and Opala volcano…

Golaya is a small basaltic stratovolcano of Pleistocene-to-Holocene age (Masurenkov, 1980) south of Asacha volcano. It is elongated in a N-S direction and overlooks small shield volcanoes and cinder cones related to regional basaltic volcanism near the headwaters of the Asacha River.

The large 15 x 25 km early Pleistocene Karymshina caldera is located SW of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatskiy and N of Gorely volcano. It produced about 800 km3 of rhyolitic ignimbrite about 1.78 million years ago, followed by rhyolitic post-caldera extrusive material (Bindeman et al, 2019).

Schmidt volcano is a large mid- to late-Pleistocene eroded shield-like volcano located N of Kronotsky volcano and SW of Gamchen (Lutchitsky, 1974). A dike complex is prominent along a NE-trending fault zone. Andreev et al.

Maly Payalpan (Little Payalpan) is a small Quaternary shield-like volcano NE of Ichinsky. Andesitic lava domes of uncertain age are located to the south. It is of basaltic andesite to andesitic composition and was constructed on top of a late-Pliocene to early Pleistocene alkaline basaltic plateau.

The Quaternary shield-like Bolshoi Payalpan (Big Payalpan) volcano is north of Ichinsky in the southern Sredinny Range. It is of dominantly basaltic andesite to andesitic composition and overlain by a late-Pleistocene to possible Holocene age basaltic cinder cones.

The small Quaternary shield-like Plosky volcano south of the Bolshaya Kimitina River is SE of Ichinsky near the SE margin of the Sredinny Range. The summit consists of a small basaltic stratovolcano overtopping the lava shield.

The late Pleistocene Akhtang Massif is located between the Bolshaya Kimitina and Kozyrevka rivers SE of Ichinsky volcano in the southern Sredinny Range. This stratovolcano is at the NE end of line of smaller monogenetic cones extending about 16 km SE. Volynets et al.

Kozyrevsky is a small Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcano located east of the Bystraya River, ~40 km E of Ichinsky in the southern Sredinny Range. It is topped by a small stratovolcano and has a large cinder cone on the SW flank.

Romanovka is a small Quaternary stratovolcano immediately north of the Kozyrevka River in the southern Sredinny Range. A broad area of cinder cones and associated lava flows is present on both sides of the river and extends primarily to the east of the volcano to the SE margin of the Sredinny Range.

The large gently dipping shield-like Uksichan volcano covers 1,850 km2, and is the largest of the Sredinny Range with a 300 km3 volume. Several dacitic domes fill the 12-km-wide central caldera; the largest of these rises 900 m above the caldera floor to form the summit.

Kulkev is a small Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcano in the southern Sredinny Range that is dwarfed by its massive neighbor immediately to the south, Uksichan.Early geological studies in the Sredinny Range (Ogorodov et al., 1972) assigned Holocene ages based on morphology, but later work noted…

Geodesistov is a small basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcano immediately WNW of the larger Anaun in the southern Sredinny Range. A small cone with a lava flow was constructed to the WSW, and a small lava field is to the south.

Anaun is a Quaternary basaltic stratovolcano NE of Uksichan in the southern Sredinny Range. A chain of NE-SW-trending cinder cones extends to the SW, and another chain of numerous cinder cones displays the same orientation S and SE of the volcano.
Krainy is a small Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcano NE of Anaun in the southern Sredinny Range. Cinder cones are found across the flanks and a lava flow is on the SW.

Kekurny is the northernmost of two overlapping small Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcanoes north of Anaun and west of Krainy volcanoes in the southern Sredinny Range. A chain of small cinder cones was constructed along a NE-SW-trending rift cutting across the volcano.

Eggella is a small basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcano on the flank of the Pleistocene Chavycha shield, west of the axis of the southern Sredinny Range. A chain of small cones on the E flank trends NE-SW.
Verkhovoy, a small Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcano in the central Sredinny Range, is dwarfed by its massive neighbor to the NNE, Alney-Chashakondzha.

Cherny is a small Quaternary stratovolcano immediately north of the massive Alney-Chashakondzha complex in the central Sredinny Range. An ENE-WSW-trending line of cinder cones was constructed on the western flank of Cherny, which is the southernmost of a cluster of small stratovolcanoes and shields trending NE from Aln…

Pogranychny is the highest and easternmost of a group of three small Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcanoes in the central Sredinny Range about 20 km NE of teh Alney-Chashakondzha complex. A chain of cinder cones extends NNE-SSW across Vodorazdelny at the N to Centralny at the SW.

A group of three small Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcanoes are present slightly east of the axis of the central Sredinny Range, about 30 km NE of Alney-Chashakondzha volcano and NNW of Lake Dvukhyurtochnoye.

Bliznets is a Quaternary basaltic stratovolcano on the crest of the central Sredinny Range SW of Kebeney volcano. Cinder cones were constructed on the E flank, and a group of cones and associated lava flows cover the northern side of the volcano.

Kebeney is a prominent Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcano in the central Sredinny Range. Two groups of NE-SW-trending cinder cones are on the SW and SE flanks, and other cinder cones are on the NE flank. Lavas surround the small eroded Kalgnitunup cone to the SW.

Fedotych, a small Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcano, is about 20 km E of the crest of the central Sredinny Range ENE of Kebeney volcano. Minor fissure-fed lava flows are located WNW.

The Quaternary Leutongey basaltic shield-like volcano is at the south end of a NE-SW-trending graben about 20 km W of the crest of the central Sredinny Range. A chain of cinder cones along the same trend cuts across the summit, and another larger cinder cone is on the S flank.

Three small overlapping Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcanoes are located NE of Leutongey volcano, west of the crest of the central Sredinny Range. Tuzovsky, the SW-most edifice, is the highest; Tvitunup is the northernmost, and Sredny is NE of Tuzovsky.

Mezhdusopochny, a Quaternary basaltic shield-like volcano, lies at the NE end of a group of small shields in a NE-SW-trending graben extending west of the crest of the Sredinny Range north of Kebeny volcano.

Shishel is a glacier-capped Quaternary basaltic shield-like volcano along the crest of the central Sredinny Range. It is on the east side of a broad graben containing a NE-SW-trending chain of overlapping small shields ranging from Leutongey on the SW to Mezhdusopochny on the NE.

Alngey, a small Quaternary stratovolcano, is immediately east of the large Pleistocene Tekletunup shield volcano, west of the crest of the northern Sredinny Range. It was constructed near the western margin of a large NE-SW-trending graben running along the axis of the Sredinny Range.

Uka, a small Quaternary basaltic shield-like volcano, was constructed near the eastern margin of a large NE-SW-trending graben along the axis of the northern Sredinny Range. It is immediately east of the crest of the Sredinny Range, opposite Alngey volcano on the western side of the graben.

Kaileney is a small Quaternary basaltic shield-like volcano near the eastern margin of a large NE-SW-trending graben running along the axis of the northern Sredinny Range. It is located NE of Uka, another shield volcano along the east side of the graben.

Plosky, a small Quaternary basaltic shield-like volcano about 20 km W of the crest of the Sredinny Range, is the westernmost volcano of the northern Sredinny Range. It is located immediately north of the large Pleistocene Tekletunup volcano.

The Quaternary basaltic Bely shield-like volcano in the northern Sredinny Range is topped by a small stratovolcano. The smaller Sergeeva and Keveneytunup shields are located to the south and east, respectively, and the late-Pleistocene Lagerny shield is to the SE.

Snezhniy is a small Quaternary basaltic shield-like volcano that was constructed near the eastern margin of a large NE-SW-trending graben running along the axis of the northern Sredinny Range. The smaller shield volcano Grechishkina is just NW, on the saddle between Snezhniy and Keveney volcanoes.

The Quaternary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like Iktunup was constructed 5 km west of the lower, but larger shield of Tunipilyakum. The two volcanoes are located immediately NW and NE, respectively, of the Pleistocene Keveney volcano.
Glacier-covered Snegovoy is a late-Quaternary shield-like volcano topped by a small basaltic cone. It was constructed about 10 km ENE of Ostry volcano, near the NE end of the Sredinny Range.

Iettunup and Lamutsky are small overlapping late-Quatenary basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcanoes at the far NE end of the Sredinny Range. The summit of Iettunup is about 7 km NW of the summit cone of Lamutsky.
Voyampolsky and Kakhtana are two basaltic to basaltic andesite shield-like volcanoes that form the NW-most volcanoes of the Sredinny Range near the headwaters of the Kakhtana River.
Vysokii and an unnamed volcano to the north are Pliocene stratovolcanoes with Pleistocene lava domes on or near their flanks (Masurenkov 1980).
Tumanniy is a Pliocene-Pleistocene shield-like volcano with flank lava domes (Masurenkov 1980).

Ded i Baba (Ded and Baba) is an early Pleistocene shield-like volcano SW of Koshelev volcano; an unnamed mid-Pleistocene volcano with a small caldera breached to the east lies between these two volcanoes (Masurenkov 1980).
Tretya Rechka is an early Pleistocene shield-like volcano with a small caldera open to the SE (Masurenkov 1980).
Pliocene to lower Pleistocene shield-like volcano (Masurenkov 1980).
Igolki and Bol'shiye Igolki are two lower to mid-Pleistocene shield-like volcanoes (Masurenkov 1980).
Pliocene to lower Pleistocene shield-like volcano (Masurenkov 1980).
Perevalny is a small upper-Pleistocene shield volcano NNE of Khodutka volcano; an unnamed Pleistocene stratovolcano is located immediately NE of Perevalny (Masurenkov 1980).
Krugliy was identified by Masurenkov (1980) as a late Pleistocene shield volcano.
Savan is a Pliocene to lower Pleistocene shield volcano (Masurenkov 1980).
Malaya Ipelka is an isolated mid to late-Pleistocene volcanic massif rising above the SW coastal lowlands north of the Opala River (Masurenkov 1980).
The conical early Pleistocene basaltic Ploskiy volcano is located west of Asacha volcano and north of a large group of late Pleistocene to Holocene pyroclastic cones (Masurenkov, 1980).
Two lower to mid-Pleistocene shield-like volcanoes (Masurenkov 1980).
Small conical late Pleistocene basaltic volcano (Masurenkov, 1980).
Tolmacheva and Utes are conical basaltic volcanoes of late-Pleistocene age (Masurenkov 1980).
Udochka is a mid-Pleistocene shield-like volcano SW of Opala (Masurenkov 1980).

Bolshaya Ipelka is a massive eroded lower Pleistocene shield-like volcano that covers a 32 x 42 km area west of the main volcanic zone of southern Kamchatka. A Holocene cinder cone on the SE flank is listed separately in this compilation.
Aak, Arik, and Pinachevsky are Pleistocene volcanoes along a ridge trending NW from Koryaksky volcano. Abnormal shallow earthquakes occurred in August 1966 (Gorel'chik, 1969).
Kupol is a Pleistocene basaltic andesite stratovolcano (Luchitsky 1974).

Two Pleistocene shield-like volcanoes are located NW of Kupol and SW of Vershkinsky volcanoes (Erlich 1985, pers. comm.). Satellite imagery in Google Earth appears to show a 6-km-diameter caldera open to the N with a later cone or dome complex on the eastern side.
Large Pleistocene stratovolcano north of Zhupanova River
Ditmara is a broad, low stratovolcano SE of Akademia Nauk caldera.
Unana stratovolcano is of Pleistocene age; hot springs on the volcano are related to tectonic faults (Erlich 1985, pers. comm.).

Satellite imagery shows a 2-km cone with an open crater that appears to be a volcanic feature about 9 km SE of the original location provided by Erlich (1985, pers. comm.), who identified this as a Pleistocene volcano. It is about 35 km NW of the Uzon caldera.
Pleistocene shield-like volcano north of Kolkhozhny volcano (Erlich 1985, pers. comm.).
Konechnaya was identified by Luchitsky (1974) as a middle to late Pleistocene shield-like volcano in the eastern Kamchatka Peninsula.
Vlasov (1967) notes postglacial activity of Konradi; later work indicates it is of Pleistocene age (Erlich 1985, pers. comm.).
Mid to upper Pleistocene shield-like volcano (Luchitsky 1974).

Iult (also spelled Iul't) is a large stratovolcano located north of Konradi volcano and NNW of the Gamchen volcanic complex. Lava domes on the lower northern and southern flanks were assigned a Holocene age by Luchitsky (1974), but Andreev et al. (1988) mapped them as late Pleistocene.
Sokol was identified by Luchitsky (1974) as a middle to late Pleistocene stratovolcano north of Konradi volcano in the eastern Kamchatka Peninsula.

Zarechny is a low, forested volcano constructed in the lake-filled lowlands between Kliuchevskoi and Shiveluch volcanoes, and immediately S of Kharchinsky volcano. The 760-m-high edifice contains two nested calderas, both breached widely to the SE.

Kharchinsky is a Pleistocene volcano immediately north of Zarechny volcano (Luchitsky, 1974) in the lowlands north of the Kamchatka River. The magnesian basaltic volcano rises 1400 m above the surrounding plains.

A group of basaltic cinder cones is located north of Kharchinsky volcano in the lowlands SW of Sheveluch volcano. The cones and lava flows cover a broad area north of Kharchinsky and form a peninsula extending into Lake Kharchinsky.
Small late Pleistocene basaltic shield volcano SW of Ichinsky volcano (Ogorodov et al., 1972).
Prodolny and Lauchan are adjacent Pleistocene shield volcanoes SW of Ichinsky volcano (Erlich 1985, pers. comm.).
Pleistocene basaltic stratovolcano, SW of Ichinsky volcano (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
The small isolated Lyzyk volcano is probably of late-Pleistocene age (Erlich 1985, pers. comm.).
Uchkoren is a small Pleistocene volcano (Erlich 1985, pers. comm.).
Two Pleistocene Icelandic shield volcanoes (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Late-Pleistocene Icelandic-type shield volcano (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Lower-Pleistocene shield volcano east of Ichinsky volcano (Erlich 1985, pers. comm.).
Group of three Pleistocene stratovolcanoes (Erlich, 1985 pers. comm.).
Early Pleistocene shield volcano (Ogorodov et al., 1972).
Late-Pleistocene Icelandic shield volcano (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Late Pleistocene shield volcano (Ogorodov et al., 1972).
Late Pleistocene shield volcano; the Krugelenky shield to the NE along the regional NE-SW trend is listed with Kapkan (Erlich 1985, pers. comm.).
Yanpat and Vetrovoy volcano to the north are late-Pleistocene Icelandic-type shield volcanoes (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Chavycha and Olka volcano to the north are mid to late-Pleistocene Icelandic-type shield volcanoes (Ogorodov et al. 1972).

Malaya Ketepana is one of several large shield volcanoes along the western margin of the Sredinny Range. Smaller Icelandic-type shield volcanoes are located on the south flank and NE of Malaya Ketepana.
Bolshoy Ketepana is a large isolated early Pleistocene shield volcano on the west side of the Sredinny Range (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Mid to late-Pleistocene shield volcano (Ogorodov et al. 1972).

The lower to mid-Pleistocene Tigilsky shield volcano (Ogorodov et al. 1972) appears to have a 2-km-wide crater just SE of the summit. An area on the W flank was previously listed as an Unnamed Holocene basaltic shield volcano.
Mid-Pleistocene shield volcano with a summit caldera (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
The mid to late-Pleistocene basaltic stratovolcanoes of Maly Alney and Polovinny are located SE of Alney volcano (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Mid-Pleistocene shield volcano with Hawaiian-type summit caldera (Ogorodov et al. 1972; Erlich 1986).
Lower-Pleistocene shield volcano with Hawaiian-type summit caldera (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Late-Pleistocene Icelandic-type shield volcano (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Late-Pleistocene Icelandic-type shield volcano (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Group of mid-Pleistocene extrusive lava domes (Erlich, 1985 pers. comm.).
Late-Pleistocene basaltic stratovolcano east of the Sredinny Range crest (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Shlen is a large mid-Pleistocene shield volcano west of the main Sredinny Range (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Tekletunup is a large eroded Pliocene to lower-Pleistocene shield volcano (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Late Pleistocene shield volcano (Ogorodov et al., 1972).
Late Pleistocene shield volcano (Ogorodov et al., 1972).

The late-Pleistocene complex stratovolcano Khuvkhoitun forms the highest peak of the northern Sredinny Range. Two small late-Pleistocene shield volcanoes are located immediately to the NE (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Keveney is a late-Pleistocene Icelandic-type shield volcano (Ogorodov et al. 1972).
Langtutkin is a late-Pleistocene Icelandic-type shield volcano east of the crest of the Sredinny Range (Ogorodov et al. 1972).

The Anjuisky (Anyuy) volcano group consists of fissure vents and small pyroclastic cones, the largest of which is 120-m high and is capped by a 300-m-wide crater. The initial fissure eruptions produced trachybasaltic lava flows 15-17 km long that covered an area of 100 km2.

Balagan-Tas is a cinder cone constructed along a fault on the SW flank of the Momskiy Mountains in the NE part of Russia's Sakha Republic. A poorly preserved crater fed subalkaline basaltic lava flows that covered an area of 4-5 km2. A Potassium-Argon date of 300,000 years was obtained (Prokopiev, 2007 pers. comm.).

Volcanism in the Vitim Volcanic Field dates back to the Miocene and covers an area of about 4,500 km2 east of the northern part of Lake Baikal. The most voluminous activity took place from the Miocene to Pleistocene. Most of the volcanic centers are located in the NW part of the field (Johnson et al., 2005).

The Tunkin Depression volcanic field (also known as the Tunka Depression) covers a broad area immediately west of the SW tip of Lake Baikal. The Khobok group of basaltic cinder cones near the village of Tunka, one of five groups of cinder cones characterized by some sources as late-Pleistocene to Holocene in age, has t…

The large East Tuva volcanic field is located WNW of the SW tip of Lake Baikal and N of the Mongolian border. The gently sloping Azas Plateau, also known as the East Tuva Plateau, the Northeast Tuva Plateau, or the Khamsara-Biykhem Plateau, covers an area of about 2,000 km2.

The Dgida Basin volcanic field, also known as the Dzhida Basin, is located south of the SW tip of Lake Baikal, near the border with Mongolia. One of a series of approximately E-W-trending depressions, the basin contains Quaternary lava flows and cinder cones ranging from 55 to 240 m in height.

The Khanuy Gol (also spelled Hanui or Hanuy Gol) Volcanic Field is also known as the Chanuj Gol or Bulgan volcanic field. It consists of a group of 10 olivine-basaltic lava and cinder cones in west-central Mongolia about 150 km WNW of the capital city of Ulaanbaatar.
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, Mongolia

The Dariganga volcanic field, located in SE Mongolia near the China border, consists of more than 200 lava and cinder cones erupted from NE-trending parallel fissures. The cones range in height from 25 to 300 m, and vary from partially eroded to completely preserved.
Northern Tibetan Plateau Volcanic Province, China

A volcanic zone spanning ~350 km E-W in NE Tibet was identified by Tong et al. (1988) as having multiple Cenozoic volcanoes. Five locations were named on the small-scale map (Yongbocuo, Bamaoqiongzhong, Kushuihuan-Beishan, Heiguotou, and Yuyiehu).
Northern Tibetan Plateau Volcanic Province, China

Listed as an unnamed Quaternary volcano by IAVCEI (1973), it was included in a summary list of northern Tibetan volcanic locations by Guo et al. (2006) under the name Heishibeihu with a cited 14C date of 670,000 years. A small shield feature is present, with a large lava field.
Northern Tibetan Plateau Volcanic Province, China

An unnamed basaltic volcano was listed in this general area by IAVCEI (1973). Although mislocated ~100 km E (1° of longitude), this entry may have been referencing the small mountain ridge of Ulagh Muztagh, ~30 km long and largely snow-covered. It was mapped as 11-4.0 Ma rhyolites in Wang et al. (2016, see citations).
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China
Longhai is a late-Cenozoic volcano (Tong et al. 1988) at the south end of the Zhemin Volcano Group of Chen (1986).
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China

The Jianghui Volcano Group consists of remnants of about 20 basaltic hills. Comparatively well-preserved craters exist along the eastern shore of Nushanhu and the western shore of Chaohu. The basalt is of early Quaternary age (Chen 1986; Whitford-Stark 1987, pers. comm.).
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China
Truncated cone of Pliocene-lower Pleistocene age (IAVCEI).

Late-Cenozoic volcano; name appears as "Tangy n" in Tong et al. (1988).

The Datong-Fengzhen volcano group, also known as Ta-T'ung or Fanjiatun, is located at the intersection of two regional fault zones. The volcanic field contains about 80 volcanic vents, including cinder cones and small lava domes. The central Datong group contains 12 cones.
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China

Tapponnier and Molnar (1977) documented from satellite images a large volcanic field with fresh features suggesting possible Holocene eruptions. Hang (1989, pers. comm.) indicates that extensive dating by Yang indicates the youngest eruptions were of late Pleistocene age.
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China

The Nuomin volcanic field, identified as Shatu in Ogara (1969) and Whiford-Stark (1987), is dominated by monogenetic cones and lava flows that cover about 600 km2 (Zhao and others, 2014). K-Ar dating by Fan and others (2012, cited in Zhao and others, 2014) indicated eruptions between 2.3 and 0.13 Ma.
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China
Jianshan volcano (at the Jianshan Farm) is located NW of the Wudalianchi volcanic field. Zhao and others (2014) reported that this isolated monogenetic cinder cone was K–Ar dated at 0.12 ± 0.02 Ma.
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China

Two adjacent volcanic cones are located just NE of the city of Kedong in the Heilongjiang Province of far northeastern of China. The larger eastern cone is about 700 m in diameter, and the smaller western one is 600 m.
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China
Dunhua was described by Whitford-Stark (1987) as being composed of flows of two or three different ages.
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, China
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, North Korea-South Korea
An area of extensive basaltic lava flows occupies a graben, the NNE-SSW-trending Ch'uga-ryong rift, that cuts diagonally across the border between North and South Korea.
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, North Korea
Central East Asia Volcanic Province, North Korea

Lava flows located between the cities of Koksan and Singye were listed as probably active in last 2,000 years by IAVCEI (1973). However, Whitford-Stark (1987) lists it as Pleistocene and Tomita (1967) states there has been no Holocene volcanism on the Korean Peninsula.
Aleutian Ridge Volcanic Arc, United States
Sergief is a small stratovolcano on SW Atka Island whose age is poorly known. The SW part of the island is older and less topographically rugged than the NE part of the island.
Aleutian Ridge Volcanic Arc, United States

Rugged pinnacles form the summit of the deeply eroded Isanotski Peaks stratovolcano, locally known as Ragged Jack, at the center of a group of three volcanoes on eastern Unimak Island. Four poorly documented eruptions were noted in the 18th and 19th centuries. However, Miller et al.
Aleutian Ridge Volcanic Arc, United States

Mount Adagdak, at the NE tip of Adak Island, lies across Andrew Lagoon from Mount Moffett volcano and ~15 km NNE of the town of Adak. It consists of a small stratovolcano capping an older shield volcano exposed on the southern side of the complex. An andesitic lava dome fills the summit crater.
Aleutian Ridge Volcanic Arc, United States
Mount Gilbert is deeply eroded and an area of former solfataric activity appears to have been glaciated. Solfataric activity had ceased between 1942 and 1945 (Byers and Barth 1953).
Aleutian Ridge Volcanic Arc, United States
Trader Mountain is a small dacitic stratocone-like feature with an extrusive dome; lava flows dip away from the center in all directions (Chris Nye, oral commun., 2007).
Alaska Peninsula Volcanic Arc, United States
The Blue Mountain lava dome cluster immediately west of Upper Ugashik Lake consists of 13 dacitic lava domes. An Ar-Ar date of about 632,000 years was obtained from the highest dome.
Alaska Peninsula Volcanic Arc, United States

An ice-scoured basaltic scoria cone and associated lava-flow apron lies at Getrude Creek about 5 km NE of Becharof Lake. The cone was constructed near the trace of the Bruin Bay fault and was Argon-Argon dated at about 500,000 years BP (Hildreth et al., 2003).
Alaska Peninsula Volcanic Arc, United States

Devils Desk, which rises 450 m above the top of Hook Glacier to its west, is the eroded neck of a former stratovolcano, most of which has been removed by extensive erosion. Three radial dikes exposed as ridges extend from the volcano toward the east.
Alaska Peninsula Volcanic Arc, United States

A group of small Pleistocene stratovolcanoes and a scoria cone lies behind the volcanic front near the headwaters of the Savonovski River, NW of the Denison to Devils Creek alignment of volcanoes. Dated ages range from about 88,000 to 390,000 years (Hildreth et al., 2003).
Alaska Peninsula Volcanic Arc, United States
Double Glacier volcano is a Pleistocene lava dome complex forming a nunatak in Double Glacier. Potassium-Argon dates range from 627 to 887 thousand years ago (Reed et al. 1992).
Northern Alaska-Bering Sea Volcanic Province, United States

Nunivak Island contains about 60 cinder cones and four maars; the surface of the island is dominated by thin pahoehoe lava flows that form a carapace over Cretaceous sedimentary rocks. The 110-km-wide permafrost-covered island lies about 30 km off the coast of SW Alaska.
Northern Alaska-Bering Sea Volcanic Province, United States

The Kookooligit Mountains are a 30 x 40 km shield volcano of Pleistocene-to-Holocene age in north-central St. Lawrence Island. The basaltic shield is composed of massive columnar-jointed lava flows overlain by more than 100 small cones (20-60 m high).
Northern Alaska-Bering Sea Volcanic Province, United States

St. George Island is comprised of Tertiary to late-Pleistocene cones and lava flows (Lee-Wong, in Wood and Kienle 1990). An eruption was reported NE of the island in 1815, but "in spite of these assertations any present volcanic activity must be regarded as doubtful" (Barth 1956).
Northern Alaska-Bering Sea Volcanic Province, United States
The Togiak volcanics are a late-Pleistocene sequence of thin lava flows that includes the subglacially formed Togiak Tuya (Wood and Kienle, 1990).
Northern Alaska-Bering Sea Volcanic Province, United States
The Ingrichuak Hills consist of at least five low lava shields of probably Quaternary age (Moll-Stalcup, in Wood and Kienle, 1990).
Northern Alaska-Bering Sea Volcanic Province, United States
Includes six vents and other scattered lava fields to south of Selawik Hills (IAVCEI) of Tertiary to Pleistocene age.
Northern Alaska-Bering Sea Volcanic Province, United States

One of the northernmost areas of Quaternary volcanism in North America, the Espenberg volcanic field, is located at the northern tip of the Seward Peninsula just south of the Arctic Circle. The five maars, the largest known on Earth, were erupted through thick permafrost during the late Pleistocene.

Massive dissected Mount Sanford shield volcano is one of the highest Quaternary volcanoes in the United States. The glacier-covered andesitic volcano towers above the Copper River and has a broad, bulbous top that is surrounded by massive, glacially excavated cirques, most prominent on the SW and SE sides of the summit…

Mount Gordon is the most prominent of a group of Pleistocene and Holocene cinder cones in the northern Wrangell Mountains SE of Tanada volcano. Most are less than 100 m high, but Gordon is a composite basaltic cinder-lava cone 5 km in diameter and 625 m high.
Alaska Peninsula Volcanic Arc, United States

Jumbo Dome is a large cylindrical plug of hornblende andesite 1.6 km long, 1.3 km wide, and 500 m high which intrudes the Devonian Keevy Peak Formation basement and overlying Tertiary Suntrana Formation (AVO, 2005-). Ar/Ar dating by Athey et al. (2006) yielded an age for Jumbo Dome of 1.026 +/- 0.057 Ma.
Northern Cordilleran Volcanic Province, United States

Prindle volcano is a small isolated basaltic cinder cone and lava flow in an area of metamorphic and granitic terrain. The cone formed sometime between the early Pleistocene and the about 1900 years before present White River ash that overlies the lava flow; Foster (in Wood and Kienle 1990) considered Prindle to be of…

The relatively small Capital Mountain andesitic shield volcano, north of Mount Sanford, contains a 4-km-wide summit caldera apparently of non-explosive origin. Shield and intracaldera lavas and dikes are dated 1-1.1 Ma (Richter, in Wood and Kienle 1990).

The westernmost volcano of the Wrangell volcanic field, Mount Drum was formed during two cycles of activity between about 750 and 250 ka, the last of which included the emplacement of an arcuate ring of ten dacitic lava domes between 350 and 250 ka (Richter et al. 1994).

Tanada Peak is an eroded remnant of an andesitic shield volcano with a former 8 x 6 km summit caldera. The 1-2 Ma old shield lavas are mostly eroded away, but younger cones are found to the north and south (Richter, in Wood and Kienle 1990).

Miller and Richter (1994) noted that Jarvis is the high point of a slightly curvilinear, N-trending, 10-km-long, 4,000-m-high ridge. The ridge, covered in snow and ice, consists of a thick sequence of dacitic and andesitic lava flows and capped by either a massive dacite flow or by a series of smaller dacite domes.
Queen Charlotte Volcano Group, United States
Mapped as Quaternary?; not likely present when glacial erosion formed inlet (Rossman 1959).
Interior Western Canada Volcanic Province, Canada
The Satah Mountain Volcanic Field on the Chilocotin-Nechako Plateau in central British Columbia consists of a N-S-trending chain of pyroclastic cones (Hickson 1990, pers. comm.).
The Kawdy Metah volcanic field lies along the Kawdy Plateau north of Level Mountain and contains a group of tuyas and subglacial mounds of Pleistocene age (Hickson et al., 1994).

The Dark Mountain volcanic field in the Cassiar Mountains consists of remnants of a group of subglacial mounds now forming volcanic rock outcrops east of Dease Lake and east of the Tuya Butte and High Tuya Lake subglacial volcanic fields (Hickson et al., 1994).

At least six vents on the Klastline Plateau, the largest of which is the volcanic neck of Castle Rock, are mapped as Quaternary and have produced linear ridges composed of subglacial piles of pillow lava and tuff-breccia (Souther, 1972).

The Hogum Range contains a group of at least 7 volcanic necks which are associated with dikes, lava flow remnants, and pyroclastic cones. Some of the cones contain striated boulders, occur in places where they would have been destroyed by Pleistocene glaciers, and are considered to be of Recent age by Lord (1948).
Eroded volcanic outcrops of Pleistocene age are found in the Alice Arm area west and north of Tseax River Cone (Hickson et al., 1994).
Interior Western Canada Volcanic Province, Canada

The Itcha Range, one of the Miocene to Pliocene felsic shield volcano complexes of the Anahim Volcanic Belt in central British Columbia, is capped by a large number of basaltic cinder cones of Pliocene to latest Pleistocene age. The highly dissected complex covers an area of 300 km2.
Interior Western Canada Volcanic Province, Canada

A group of pyroclastic cones of Pliocene to Quaternary age are located near Quesnel Lake. The Abbott Creek Cone, about 6.5 km N of Quesnel Lake, was given an Ar-Ar age of 180 ka by Kuehn et al. (2015), confirming the Quaternary activity.
Interior Western Canada Volcanic Province, Canada

The Chilcotin basalts form an extensive series of flat-lying lava flows of Miocene to Pleistocene age covering the interior of British Columbia (Mathews, 1989). The flow remnants form eroded volcanic outcrops that appear to have been erupted from now-eroded coalescing small shield volcanoes scattered throughout the int…

The Squamish volcanic field contains the southernmost vents of the Garibaldi volcanic belt. Late Pleistocene eruptions formed The Castle, a dramatic strongly jointed spire above the town of Squamish formed by ice contact lava extrusion (Mathews, 1958), and Watts Point, on Howe Sound south of Squamish, formed by subglac…
Interior Western Canada Volcanic Province, Canada

The southern part of the Miocene to Pleistocene Chicotin basalts forming an extensive series of basaltic lava flows covering much of the Thompson Plateau and Okanagan Highland in the interior of southern British Columbia are referred to as the Chilcotin Group-South.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Tumac Mountain cinder cone north of White Pass was mapped as Holocene by Simmons et al. (1983). However, tephra studies by Schasse (1987) indicated that the last eruption was 20-30,000 years before present.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

The deeply eroded Goat Rocks stratovolcano was active between about 2.5 and 0.5 million years ago (Ma) (Swanson, in Wood and Kienle 1990). The andesitic volcano was constructed over older products of a major rhyolitic explosive eruption.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Marble Mountain, an andesitic shield volcano SE of Mount St. Helens and N of Swift Reservoir, was last active about 160,000 years ago (Wood and Kienle, 1990).
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

The Simcoe volcanic field, of Pliocene-to-Pleistocene age, lies east and SE of Mount Adams. Small shield volcanoes and cinder cones, many erupted along N-S fissures, range in age to about 500,000 years old.
High Lava Plains Volcanic Province, United States

The Lava Mountain lava field is the middle of a group of three young basaltic fields located in the High Lava Plains SE of Newberry volcano. In contrast to the small fissure vents of the adjacent Devils Garden lava field, the Lava Mountain field consists of a shield volcano capped by the Lava Mountain pyroclastic cone…
High Lava Plains Volcanic Province, United States

The Four Craters Lava Field is the SE-most of a group of three basaltic lava fields SE of Newberry volcano in the High Lava Plains of central Oregon. The lava field originated from four pyroclastic cones that were constructed along a roughly 4-km-long NW-SE-trending line.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

The Boring Lava volcanic field, underlying part of the city of Portland, Oregon, and neighboring areas to the east and across the Columbia River in Washington, was active from the Pliocene until about the mid-Pleistocene.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Mount Defiance, an andesitic shield volcano, lies south of the Columbia River Gorge and SW of the town of Hood River, Oregon.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Andesitic Lost Lake Butte shield volcano lies NW of Mount Hood volcano and overlooks Lost Lake.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Mount Wilson is the most prominent of a group of Pleistocene shield volcanoes between Olallie Butte and Mount Hood (Sherrod, in Wood and Kienle, 1990). Summit Butte shield volcano lies to the SW and Clear Lake Butte to the NW.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Ollalie Butte is a basaltic andesite shield volcano that is older than about 25,000 years before present. North Pinhead cinder cone to the north is younger, but its flows are glaciated, suggesting an age of more than 11,000 years (Sherrod, in Wood and Kienle 1990).
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Three Fingered Jack is a distinctive deeply eroded basaltic andesite shield volcano that forms the highest peak between Mt. Jefferson and the Three Sisters. A pyroclastic cone buttressed by radial dikes forms its sharp-ridged summit.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Black Butte is a prominent small stratovolcano east of the Cascade Range crest. Despite its youthful profile, Black Butte is older than many other Cascade Range stratovolcanoes because of its position in a rain shadow to the east. Potassium-Argon dates average around 0.45 million years ago (Taylor, 1981).
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Mount Washington is an eroded Pleistocene basaltic andesite shield volcano capped by a steep-sided central plug that is the most prominent landmark between North Sister and Three Fingered Jack volcanoes.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Black Crater is a Pleistocene basaltic andesite shield volcano SE of Belknap volcano. Trout Creek Butte volcano lies to the SE of Black Crater, and scattered Pleistocene cinder cones lie to the NE.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Scott Mountain is a Pleistocene basaltic andesite shield volcano lying SW of Belknap volcano.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
The Tumalo volcanic center is the inferred source of large-volume Pleistocene ashflows such as the Desert Spring Tuff, the Bend Pumice and Tumalo Tuff, and the Shevlin Park Tuff.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Broken Top is a complex dominantly basaltic andesite stratovolcano immediately SE of South Sister volcano. It is extensively eroded by glaciers, with the summit crater breached to the SE. Intermittent eruptions of andesite, dacite, and rhyolite have produced lava flows, pyroclastic flows, and airfall tephra.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Williamson Mountain, the highest of a group of small Pleistocene shield volcanoes or large cinder cones SW of Mount Bachelor, is flanked by Elk Mountain to the north and Sixbit Point to the WSW.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Irish Mountain, a Pleistocene shield volcano SW of Williamson Mountain, was roughly estimated to be 0.25-0.73 million years (Sherrod, in Wood and Kienle, 1990). A N-S-trending chain of cinder cones cuts across Irish Mountain.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
The Pleistocene Taylor Butte shield volcano lies SW of Irish Mountain. A chain of N-S-trending cinder cones lies SSW of Taylor Butte.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
The Wuksi Butte-Twin Lakes volcanic field is a 7-km-long N-S trending chain SW of Lookout Mountain consisting of scoria cones at the north and three tuff rings up to 1 km in diameter at the south.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Cupit Mary Mountain, a basaltic andesite shield volcano west of Waldo Lake, has K-Ar dates of 0.3 and 0.68 million years (Sherrod, in Wood and Kienle, 1990).
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Fuji Mountain shield volcano SW of Waldo Lake was considered to of Pleistocene age (Sherrod, in Wood and Kienle, 1990). Mount Ray to the ENE, south of Waldo Lake is reversely polarized and older than 0.73 million years.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Maiden Peak is the highest and southernmost of a chain of Pleistocene shield volcanoes and pyroclastic cones extending from north of Odell Lake to Charlton Butte.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Red Top Mountain and Lakeview Mountain shield volcanoes of Pleistocene age lie between Odell and Crescent Lakes.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

The glacially modified Cowhorn and Sawtooth Mountain shield volcanoes and adjacent cinder cones lie SW of Crescent Lake. A lava from Sawtooth Mountain, located SW of Cowhorn Mountain was K-Ar dated at 0.56 and 0.52 million years (Sherrod, in Wood and Kienle, 1990).
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Cappy Mountain is a large, dissected mid-Pleistocene stratovolcano NNE of Mt. Thielson and south of Crescent Lake with rhyodacitic lavas around its flanks.
High Lava Plains Volcanic Province, United States
China Hat and the adjacent East Butte silicic lava domes, located ESE of Newberry volcano, have K-Ar dates of 800,000 and 870,000 years BP, respectively.
High Lava Plains Volcanic Province, United States
Quartz Butte lava-dome complex, ESE of the China Hat-East Butte lava domes, have a K-Ar date of 1.1 million years.

A large group of tuff rings, tuff cones, and maars occupies the Fort Rock-Christmas Lake Valley basin S of Newberry volcano. The eroded central plug of Mount Thielsen forms a prominent summit spire known as the "Lightning Rod of the Cascades." The heavily eroded volcano is Potassium-Argon dated about 0.29 million years ago (Sherrod, in Wood and Kienle 1990).

Mount Bailey is the southernmost of a N-S chain of volcanoes west of Diamond Lake. Volcanism migrated to the south, with Mount Bailey being late Pleistocene in age, between 100,000 and 11,000 years before present (Sherrod, in Wood and Kienle 1990).

Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The basaltic-to-dacitic Sprague River Valley volcanic field consists of small shield volcanoes, cinder cones, and about two dozen maars active from 5-1.5 million years ago (Sherrod, in Wood and Kienle, 1990).

Pelican Butte, one of the largest volcanoes between Crater Lake and Mount Shasta, is a late Pleistocene andesitic shield volcano. Mount McLoughlin is a large basaltic andesite lava cone containing a pyroclastic core exposed by glaciation that is capped by an armor of andesitic lava flows from summit and flank vents.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Brown Mountain, SE of Mount McLoughlin, is a forested basaltic andesite shield volcano with fresh, unvegetated lava flows descending as far as the base of the volcano on three sides.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

The Mountain Lakes volcanic field, located east of Brown Mountain and NW of Klamath Falls, is a Pliocene-to-Quaternary cluster of andesitic volcanic vents. The volcanic field contains Aspen Butte and Little Aspen Butte, the latter a shield volcano that is the southernmost Quaternary volcano in Oregon (Hildreth, 2007).

The Silver Creek volcanic field covers about 1600 km2 ESE of Newberry volcano and Diamond Craters. Four K-Ar dates in the eastern part of the field range from 3 to 2 million years, but the youngest rocks could be Pleistocene in age (Wood and Kienle, 1990).
High Lava Plains Volcanic Province, United States

The Lava Butte shield volcano, also known as Rocky Butte, lies south of Jordan Craters, and is 0.03-0.09 million years old (Hart and Mertzman, 1983). The slightly older Clarks Butte shield lies to the north and has been dated at 0.25 million years. Another unnamed shield volcano lies to the east of Lava Butte.
High Lava Plains Volcanic Province, United States

Jackies Butte, sometimes referred to as Bowden Crater, is a small, relatively unstudied basaltic volcanic field located near the SE corner of Oregon with two small shield volcanoes and two cinder cones.

Brushy Butte forms a small shield complex immediately east of Timbered Crater, SSE of the Medicine Lake Highlands. A group of cinder cones near Pleistocene Burney Mountain volcano, including Twin Buttes to the SE, is part of an area of extensive Quaternary volcanism north of the Lassen volcanic center. Lava flows from two isolated cinder cones in the Silver Lake Volcanic Field NW of Lassen Peak blocked drainages, forming three small lakes. The cones lie SW of Burney Mountain and WNW of MaGee Peak.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

A line of cinder cones along a NNW-SSE fissure produced a series of lava flows. Bear Wallow Butte, the source of unvegetated lava flows on its eastern and western flanks, lies at the southern end of the chain.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Eagle Lake volcanic field occupies the junction of the Cascades, Sierra Nevada, and Basin and Range geologic provinces, and consists of 15 cinder cones and basaltic lava flow vents within a larger Quaternary basaltic field.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
The Golden Trout Creek volcanic field consists of a group of Quaternary alkali olivine basalt cinder cones and lava flows in the Toowa Valley about 25 km S of Mount Whitney.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Coso Volcanic Field, located E of the Sierra Nevada Range at the western edge of the Basin and Range province, consists of Pliocene to Quaternary rhyolitic lava domes and basaltic cinder cones covering a 400 km2 area. Much of the field lies within the China Lake Naval Weapons Center.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Lavic Lake basaltic volcanic field was considered to contain four Holocene cinder cones, three in the Lavic Lake area and a fourth in the Rodman Mountains 20 km to the west (Miller, 1989), but later work by USGS scientists revised that evaluation to late-Pleistocene.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Lava flows from two cinder cones near Copco Lake were dated from morphological evidence as being less than one or two thousand years old (Williams 1949), however Miller (1989) indicated that the Copco Lake volcanics are of late-Pleistocene age.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
The Goosenest shield volcano and summit pyroclastic cone were considered by Williams (1949) to be Holocene in age, but Miller (1989) mapped it as late Pleistocene.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States

Williams (1949) mapped the Whaleback shield volcano and nearby fissure vents as Holocene in age, but Luedke and Smith (1981) mapped the area as Pleistocene and Miller (1989) did not include Whaleback in a summary of Holocene volcanism in California.
High Cascades Volcanic Arc, United States
Rainbow Mountain, located between Mt. Shasta and Medicine Lake volcanoes, is a massive andesitic-dacitic stratovolcano of early Pleistocene age.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

Hackamore is a large volcanic field east of Medicine Lake volcano. This Quaternary field covers an area of at least 850 km2 with at least a dozen vents, the youngest of which is about 600,000 years old (Hildreth, 2007).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Big Cave shield volcano, at the northern end of an area of late-Quaternary volcanism extending north from Lassen Peak, is a small basaltic shield with young pyroclastic cones at the summit and north flank.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
The Cinder Butte shield volcano and flank pyroclastic cones was listed as latest Pleistocene or Holocene (Sarna-Wojcicki et al. 1983), and as Holocene by Luedke and Smith (1981) and Miller (1989).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Burney Mountain, a large dacitic lava-dome complex, was active about 0.23 million years ago (Clynne, in Wood and Kienle, 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
The Snow Mountain volcanic center is a large eroded andesitic-to-rhyolitic stratovolcano that was active from about 2 million to 1 million years ago (Clynne, in Wood and Kienle, 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Magee Peak, an eroded andesitic stratovolcano, was active about 1-2 million years ago (Clynne, in Wood and Kienle, 1990). The andesitic Freaner Peak shield volcano lies across a saddle to the NE.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Blacks Mountain, 25 km east of Hat Creek, is the most prominent of a group of andesitic shield volcanoes and is 1-2 million years old (Clynne, in Wood and Kienle, 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Potato Butte cinder cone and lava field, including the Hat Creek lava flow that traveled nearly 30 km from a fissure vent near the town of Old Station, lies immediately north of the Lassen volcanic center.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Latour Butte, an andesitic lava cone NW of Lassen National Park, was probably active 1-2 million years ago (Clynne, in Wood and Kienle, 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Caribou volcanic field east of Lassen National Park contains about 140 mid-Pleistocene to late-Pleistocene cones and shields that are controlled by Basin and Range extensional faulting. The Caribou volcanic field was active from about 450,000 to 20,000 years ago (Hildreth, 2007).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

A massive lava Pleistocene lava flow from Red Lake Mountain cinder cone traveled nearly 30 miles (~45 km) to the west. The basaltic flow covers nearly 50 sq miles and has an estimated volume of 1-2 cu miles (Macdonald, 1963). Highway 44 traverses the flow.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

Table Mountain, an andesitic stratovolcano at the NW corner of Lassen National Park, is an andesitic stratovolcano active about 1-2 million years ago. Red Lake Mountain, immediately to the NW of Table Mountain, is the source of youthful-looking basaltic and andesitic lava flows of late-Pleistocene age (Clynne, in Wood…
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Black Butte is a late Pleistocene pyroclastic cone west of Lassen National Park (Miller, 1989).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Dittmar volcanic center is a massive eroded andesitic stratovolcano at the SE part of Lassen National Park that was active about 2.-5-1 million years ago (Clynne, 1990). Dacitic lava domes are located in the Hot Springs and Kings Creek canyons.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Sifford Mountain, a basaltic-to-andesitic shield volcano, rises in south-central Lassen National Park. It was probably active during the past 100,000 years (Clynne, in Wood and Kienle, 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The massive, highly eroded Maidu volcano center SW of Lassen National Park was active about 2-0.8 million years ago (Clynne, 1990). The hydrothermally altered andesitic stratovolcano also has erupted rhyolitic rocks, and a dacitic lava-dome field lies on the north flank of the volcanic center.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Inskip Hill and nearby pyroclastic cones were thought to be of Holocene age, but later mapping indicates a late Pleistocene age (Miller, 1989).
California Coast Ranges Volcano Group, United States

The isolated Sutter Buttes rise above the flat floor of the Sacramento Valley. This andesitic-to-rhyolitic lava-dome complex was active during the Pleistocene. An andesitic central core is surrounded by a ring of dacitic-to-rhyolitic domes.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
The large 17 x 32 km Long Valley caldera east of the central Sierra Nevada Range formed as a result of the voluminous Bishop Tuff eruption about 760,000 years ago.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Big Pine (Aberdeen) volcanic field in the Owens Valley contains more than 40 vents over a 1,000 km2 region of the Owens Valley. The basaltic field consists of cinder cones that produced lava flows up to 9 km long and a single rhyolitic lava dome. Activity was episodic throughout the Quaternary.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Cima volcanic field covers an area of about 150 km2 and contains 52 vents of Miocene-to-Pleistocene age. The youngest flows have been mapped as Holocene (Calif Div of Mines & Geol), and a radiocarbon date of 330-480 BP was obtained on the Black Tank cone.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The 70-sq-km Amboy basaltic lava field was erupted onto a flat-lying alluvial valley from Amboy Crater, a prominent cinder cone with four nested craters that rises 75 m above adjacent lava flows at the NE end of the lava field.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

Remnants of Pleistocene or Holocene basaltic flows and pyroclastic deposits lie on alluvium (Chesterman 1982). These volcanics are mapped as Pleistocene (Calif Div Mines & Geol, Luedke and Smith 1981).
High Lava Plains Volcanic Province, United States

A Pleistocene shield volcano and tuff cone in the western Snake River Plain, Sinker Butte, is partially dissected by the Snake River Canyon. Lava flows from the tuff cone flowed up to 10 km to the south. A broad lava shield is overlain by a large tuff cone that is capped with lava flows and welded spatter.
High Lava Plains Volcanic Province, United States

This extensive field of Quaternary basalt extends about 95 km between Mountain Home and the Kuna-Melba area southeast of the Boise River Valley (Wood, 1997). Basaltic outcrops have been dated around 2 Ma at Wild Horse Butte and Jackass Butte.
Yellowstone-Snake River Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

Several late-Pleistocene lava flows were erupted near Big Southern Butte. The North Robbers flow was radiocarbon dated 11,940 +/- 300 before present (BP); the Cerro Grande flow was dated at 10,780 +/- 300 BP.
Yellowstone-Snake River Hotspot Volcano Group, United States
The Blackfoot Volcanic Field (BVF) is a Quaternary volcanic field in SE Idaho around Blackfoot Reservoir, within a graben of the Northern Basin and Range Province.
Yellowstone-Snake River Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

North and South Menan Buttes are the two largest of a N-S line of basaltic tuff cones formed by phreatomagmatic eruptions along the Snake River in eastern Idaho. The larger N cone is ~2 km in diameter, and 3 km from the S cone (using crater centers).
Yellowstone-Snake River Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

The Yellowstone Plateau volcanic field developed through three volcanic cycles spanning two million years that included some of the world's largest known eruptions. Eruption of the over 2,450 km3 Huckleberry Ridge Tuff about 2.1 million years ago created the more than 75-km-long Island Park caldera.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
The Leucite Hills consist of a 2000 km2 area with less than two dozen isolated lava flows, dikes, necks and cinder cones of unusual potassium-rich composition. Their age is about 1.1 Ma.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Several Quaternary lava flows along the Nevada-Oregon border issued from small shield volcanoes. The only available Potassium-Argon age is 1.2 million years ago.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

A group of cinder cones and lava flows in the Buffalo Valley north of the Oligocene Fish Creek Mountains caldera range in age from 3.05 to 0.92 million years ago (Dohrenwend, in Wood and Kienle 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

A small volcanic field of rhyolitic lava domes and flows about 20 km S of Reno, Nevada, ranges in age from 2.53 to 1.14 million years. No eruptive activity has occurred during the Holocene, although it was included in the Catalog of Active Volcanoes of the World (Coombs and Howard, 1960) based on its geothermal activit…
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

Aurora-Bodie volcanic field in west-central Nevada near the California border NNE of Mono Lake contains well-preserved cinder cones and lava flows of late Pleistocene age. The most prominent feature, Aurora Crater, is a 25,000 years before present cinder cone surrounded by lava flows.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Lunar Crater volcanic field in central Nevada contains almost 100 Pliocene-Pleistocene volcanic vents cutting across the Oligocene Lunar Lake caldera. The most distinctive feature of the field is Lunar Crater, a 1-km-wide, 130-m-deep maar.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

A solitary cinder cone in Clayton Valley NE of Silver Peak is Potassium-Argon dated about 0.39 million years ago. The breached cone has produced a 2-km-long lava flow partly buried by Quaternary alluvium (Dohrenwend, in Wood and Kienle 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Crater Flat volcanic field south of the Miocene Timber Mountain caldera contains five Quaternary cinder cones and lava flows. The youngest, Lathrop Wells scoria cone, was formed about 80,000 years ago (Valentine et al., 2007) and produced lava flows from vents at the S and NE flanks of the cone.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

A Pliocene-to-Quaternary volcanic field north of St. George in SW Utah contains numerous cinder cones and lava flows. The Santa Clara lava flow, originating from two youthful-looking cinder cones above Snow Canyon, is one of many young late-Quaternary lava flows in the Colorado Plateau/Basin and Range region.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

Bald Knoll is the youngest of a group of basaltic cinder cones on the SW part of the Paunsaugunt Plateau in southern Utah, between the southern end of Bryce Canyon National Park and the western margin of Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The basaltic Kolob volcanic field on the west margin of Zion National Park contains the youthful-looking Crater Hill cinder cone and associated lava flows at the SW corner of the park and older cones to the north on the upper Kolob Plateau.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Pleistocene Mineral Mountains-Cove Fort volcanic field includes silicic lava domes in the Mineral Mountains and basaltic and basaltic andesite cinder cones and lava flows of the Cove Fort and adjacent areas.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Smelter Knolls in west-central Utah are a Pliocene rhyolitic lava dome complex. Nearby basaltic volcanism is dated at 0.31 million years ago (Nash, in Wood and Kienle 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
The Quaternary basaltic andesite shield volcano Fumarole Butte in west-central Utah is dated 0.9 million years ago. Hot springs are found on the eastern flanks (Nash, in Wood and Kienle 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Willow Peak cinder cone is located in the White River National Forest, and can be reached from Coffee Pot Road. Although geomorphically young, this cone is regarded as somewhat older than the Dotsero lava flow (about 4,000 years before present). A lava flow that traveled 5.5 km to the east.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
A 6.5-km-long basaltic lava flow from two scoria cones is Potassium-Argon dated 0.64 +/- 0.2 million years ago (Larson et al. 1975).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
The Sentinel Plain volcanic field covers about 600 km2 along the Gila River with basaltic lava flows. The field was active from 3.3 to possibly 1.3 million years ago (Lynch, in Wood and Kienle 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Springerville Volcanic Field contains more than 380 vents and lava flows of Pliocene to Pleistocene age. This alkali basalt field contains cinder cones, maars and lava domes, with the youngest dated cones being 0.3 million years ago.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The small San Carlos volcanic field covers about 50 km2 with basaltic cinder cone and lava flow remnants. The field, active from possibly 4.2 to 1.0 million years ago, is located within the San Carlos Apache Indian reservation (Lynch, in Wood and Kienle 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Geronimo (San Bernardino) volcanic field contains over 140 eruptive centers, mostly pyroclastic cones, in an area of 850 km2. The basaltic field in the SE corner of Arizona was active between 3.2 and 0.3 million years ago (Lynch, in Wood and Kienle 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Potrillo volcanic field, in southern New Mexico along the western margin of the Rio Grande Rift, contains more than 150 cinder cones and five maars. Features include Kilbourne Hole, a small shield volcano, and Potrillo maar, which straddles the US-Mexico border.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Jornada del Muerto volcanic field in south-central New Mexico consists of a low shield that was the source of large radial lava flows. The age of the lavas is 0.76 million years (Crumpler and Aubele; in Wood and Kienle, 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Miocene to Pleistocene Lucero volcanic field contains basaltic cinder cones, small shield volcanoes and tuff rings scattered over a 2000 km2 area. The latest eruptions took place only a few tens of thousand years ago (Baldridge, in Wood and Kienle, 1990).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
Mapped as Pleistocene or Pliocene flows. Probably early Pleistocene (Lipman and Moench, 1972).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
The Cat Hills volcanic field west of Albuquerque contains about two dozen small cinder cones erupted along a N-S fissure, a small shield volcano and a Pliocene maar.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Albuquerque Volcanic Field was erupted along N-S fissures from about 0.17 to 0.7 million years ago, producing spatter cones and lava flows (Kudo, in Wood and Kienle, 1990). Vulcan (or J) cone contains a lava dome split into two by an explosion crater.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States
The 22-km-wide Valles Caldera was formed as a result of two large-volume eruptions that created the widespread Bandelier Tuff ignimbrite plateaus on all sides of the caldera.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The massive Taos Plateau volcanic field covers an area of 7000 km2 along the Rio Grande Rift in north-central New Mexico and was active from about 10 million to 1.8 million years ago. The Red Hill lava flow is of probable Pleistocene age (Dungan et al., 1989).
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Ocate (Mora) volcanic field is part of the Jemez Lineament and located east of the Rio Grande Rift in northern New Mexico. It contains numerous basaltic to dacitic flows and cinder cones over a 90 km2 area.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, United States

The Raton-Clayton volcanic field is a large Miocene-Quaternary field stretching from near Trinidad, Colorado to Clayton, New Mexico. The main pulse of volcanism took place between 4 and 1.8 million years ago.
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

Water discoloration, sulfur odor, possible boiling water, and possible minor floating pumice were observed 60 km NW of the tip of Oahu on 22 May 1956. The seamount at that location has a depth of about 1,200 m at the end of the Kaena Ridge.
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States
The oldest of the volcanoes comprising the island of Hawaii, Kohala forms an oval shield constructed along two NW-SE trending rift zones at the NW tip of the island.
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

The uninhabited island of Kahoolawe, SW of the island of Maui, consists of a broad, low basaltic shield volcano formed by Pleistocene eruptions along a rift zone that extends SW from a buried, 5-km-wide caldera at the eastern side of the island. The eastern rim of the caldera lies beneath the waters of Kanapou Bay.
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States
The Pleistocene Mahukona seamount lies between the islands of Hawaii and Kahoolawe, NW of Hualalai volcano. The distinct cone is about 4 km in diameter.
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

The Pleistocene West Maui shield volcano is deeply dissected by spectacular steep-sided valleys that extend from the north and east into the summit caldera. Late-stage cinder cones and lava flows on the W flank were mapped as Recent by Stearns (1946). Mullineaux et al.
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

The Pleistocene Lanai shield volcano was constructed along three rift zones, the most prominent of which is the NW rift zone. The large submarine Clark debris avalanche extended 150 km S (Moore et al. 1989). A caldera is located at the southern end of the island.
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

East Molokai volcano was constructed along an E-W trending rift zone. The northern half of the volcano is truncated by a cliff more than 1 km high resulting from the massive Wailau debris avalanche that extended more than 100 km N (Moore et al. 1989).
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

The flat West Molokai shield volcano was formed by eruptions along two rift zones at the west end of Molokai Island during the Pliocene and early Pleistocene. The youngest Potassium-Argon date is 1.52 +/- 0.6 million years ago (Langenheim and Clague, 1987).
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

The extensively eroded, elongated Koolau basaltic shield volcano of Pliocene-to-Pleistocene age forms much of the eastern half of Oahu Island. A lengthy NW rift zone is defined by a dike complex that runs the length of the windward coast.
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States
The elongated Waianae shield volcano forms much of western Oahu Island. The Waianae Slump, a landslide formed during multiple events, extends 90 km SW (Moore et al. 1989).
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States

Kauai Island is composed of a single large eroded shield volcano with a summit caldera 15-20 km in diameter and two flank calderas. Large Pliocene debris avalanches extended to the north and south. The spectacular Waimea Canyon and Napalm cliffs on the NW coast are products of extensive erosion.
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States
Niihau is the eroded remnant of a Miocene to Pliocene shield volcano. Rejuvenation during the late Pliocene and Pleistocene produced a series of small shield volcanoes, cinder cones and tuff cones.
Hawaiian-Emperor Hotspot Volcano Group, United States
Ka'ula Island is a Pleistocene tuff cone that rests on a broad submerged shield volcano (Macdonald and Abbott, 1970; IAVCEI, 1973).

The Marquesas Islands show an age progression with the youngest volcanoes occurring at the SE end of the chain. Hiva Oa, a large shield volcano with a caldera truncated on the south side, is the NW-most volcano of the chain with some Pleistocene activity.

Fatu Hiva is the SE-most and youngest of the Marquesas Islands. Potassium-Argon dates for the island, a shield volcano with a large summit caldera truncated on the west, range from 1.39-1.30 million years ago (Duncan and Mcdougall, 1974).
Society Islands Hotspot Volcano Group, France

Like several other central Pacific island chains, the Society Islands are progressively younger to the SE. Moorea, the NW-most of the Society Islands with Pleistocene volcanism, is a dissected shield volcano whose caldera is open to the north and surrounded by sharp-topped peaks.
Society Islands Hotspot Volcano Group, France

Tahiti-Nui is the larger of two coalescing shield volcanoes forming the island of Tahiti. Much of the original volcano is intact; the central caldera is drained to the north by the Papenoo River. Potassium-Argon dates range from 1.23-0.48 million years ago (Duncan and Mcdougall, 1976).
Society Islands Hotspot Volcano Group, France

The smaller and younger of two coalescing shield volcanoes on Tahiti, Tahiti-Iti (Taiarapu) is connected to Tahiti-Nui by a narrow isthmus. Potassium-Argon ages range from 0.48-0.38 million years ago (Duncan and Mcdougall 1976).
Austral-Cook Hotspot Volcano Group, New Zealand
Volcanic rocks of Aitutaki Atoll in the Cook Islands are Potassium-Argon dated 0.77-0.66 million years ago (Duncan and Mcdougall 1976).
Austral-Cook Hotspot Volcano Group, New Zealand
Potassium-Argon dates from the Rarotonga shield volcano in the Cook Islands range from 1.8-1.2 million years ago (Duncan and Mcdougall 1976).

Rurutu is an eroded shield volcano in the Austral (Tubuai) Islands capped by later Pleistocene lava flows that reached the sea through gaps in the fringing coral reef. The younger volcanics are Potassium-Argon dated from 1.85-1.05 million years ago (Duncan and McDougall, 1976).
Pitcairn Hotspot Volcano Group, United Kingdom

Located at the SE end of the Duke of Gloucester-Gabbier Islands chain, Pitcairn is a small island remnant of a shield volcano with a dissected caldera. Potassium-Argon dates range from 0.95-0.45 million years ago (Duncan et al. 1974).
Campbell Plateau Volcanic Province, New Zealand

The isolated, uninhabited Antipodes Islands are located in the south Pacific, 770 km SE of New Zealand. Volcanism has been dominantly pyroclastic, and the presence of well-preserved scoria cones suggests a Holocene age (LeMasurier and Thomson, 1990).
Gulf of California Rift Volcanic Province, Mexico

The Cerro Prieto Volcanic Complex is the surface manifestation of the Cerro Prieto Geothermal Field, and 90 km NW of the Gulf of California and 35 km S of the city of Mexicali. As described by García-Sánchez et al.
Gulf of California Rift Volcanic Province, Mexico

San Quintín Volcanic Field on the NW coast of Baja California consists of 11 late-Pleistocene pyroclastic cones and related lava flows. Low lava shields, initially submarine, are capped by scoria cones.
Gulf of California Rift Volcanic Province, Mexico
Volcán Coronado is a roughly 440-m-high, 2-km-diameter volcanic cone at the northern end of the 7-km-long Coronado Island, 3 km off the E coast of Baja California in the Canal de los Ballenas.
Gulf of California Rift Volcanic Province, Mexico

The Tres Vírgenes volcanic complex contains the only large stratovolcanoes in Baja California, rising above the Gulf of California in the east-central part of the peninsula. Three volcanoes, El Viejo, El Azufre, and La Vírgen, constructed along a NE-SW line, are progressively younger to the SW.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, Mexico
Isla Isabel, a complex of tuff cones and associated lava flows, forms a small 1.5-km-long island located in the Pacific Ocean 30 km off the coast of Narayit state, NW of the city of Tepic, Mexico.

The steep-sided Papayo lava dome and related dacitic lava flows was emplaced in a NE-SW oriented depression south of Telapon and north of Iztaccíhuatl in the Sierra Nevada range west of Mexico City. The lava flows extended about 10 km both WSW and ENE from the dome that rises about 230 m above the flows.

Los Atlixcos, also known as Cerro el Abra, consists of a broad area of lava flows topped by two large cones at the eastern end of the Mexican Volcanic Belt along the Gulf of Mexico about 80 km NW of the city of Veracruz, near Palma Sola.

Cofre de Perote is a massive Quaternary andesitic-dacitic volcano at the NNE end of a volcanic chain extending southward to Pico de Orizaba (Citlaltépetl). Lava flows dominated the formation of this broad massif, which is largely of Pleistocene age.

A broad area of Quaternary volcanic rocks lies in the highland between Cofre de Perote and Las Cumbres volcanoes. Two large arcuate E-facing scarps of uncertain origin, possibly eroded volcanic centers, are the most prominent features of the La Gloria volcanic field.

Las Cumbres volcanic complex is a Quaternary center ~15 km NNE of Pico de Orizaba The ~3.5 km summit caldera is narrowly breached on the E, and is largely filled by a dacitic lava dome (Cerro Gordo or El Cumbre Grande). Eruptive activity at the main complex ceased during the late Pleistocene.
Gulf of California Rift Volcanic Province, Mexico

Cerro León, also known as Volcán Prieto ("Dark volcano"), is a small, roughly 280-m-high cone of early Pleistocene age (~2.5 Ma) that was constructed along the Guaymas lineament on the east coast of northern Baja California (Martin-Barajas and Weber, 2003).
Gulf of California Rift Volcanic Province, Mexico

The San Ignacio volcanic field lies north of the town of the same name and east of the town of Vizcaino. Miocene tholeiitic basaltic-andesitic lava flows and somewhat magnesian Pliocene-to-Pleistocene andesites emitted from dozens of cinder cones overlie Tertiary sediments (Pallares et al., 2007; Calmus et al., 2003).
Gulf of California Rift Volcanic Province, Mexico
El Aguajito caldera (also known as Santa Ana caldera) is located along the Gulf of California immediately NE of Tres Vírgenes volcano and NW of La Reforma caldera.
Gulf of California Rift Volcanic Province, Mexico

Punta Púlpito is a Pleistocene obsidian dome dated at about 0.5 million years that forms a small peninsula along the Gulf of California, east of the southern tip of Bahía Concepción in southern Baja California.
Gulf of California Rift Volcanic Province, Mexico

The Cerro Mencenares volcanic complex along the Gulf of California is situated at the northern extent of the Loreto Basin, SE of Bahia Concepcion (Dorsey and Umhoefer, 2000). It's eruptive history, which involves three eruptive events, likely played a role in the development of the Loreto Basin.
Gulf of California Rift Volcanic Province, Mexico

The early Pleistocene La Reforma caldera lies along the Gulf of California immediately east of Tres Vírgenes volcano and SE of the late Pleistocene El Aguajito caldera. The roughly 9-km-wide caldera contains basaltic, andesitic, and dacitic lava flows, and rhyolitic lava domes.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, Mexico

The Moctezuma volcanic field occupies a 380 km2 area along the foothills of the Sierra Madre Occidental in NW México. An early stage of tholeiitic basaltic volcanism originating from fissures along the eastern boundary of the graben produced a broad mesa within a large graben in the Moctezuma Basin.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, Mexico

The Camargo volcanic field is located in the northern Bolsón de Mapimí graben in north-central México, about 150 km SW of Big Bend National Park in Texas. More than 300 volcanic vents, mostly cinder cones and lava cones, are located in a broad 2,500 km2 lava plateau that extends 60 km E-W and 70 km N-S.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, Mexico

An area of Quaternary phonolitic and basaltic pyroclastic cones and lava flows is located along the Gulf of Mexico SE of the Sierra de Tamaulipas. Trachytic and phonolitic eruptions were followed by the emission of young basaltic lava flows from cinder cones.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, Mexico

The Tertiary-to-Quaternary Los Flores volcanic field is located in the rugged limestone peaks of the Sierra Madre Oriental at the conjunction of the states of Tamaulipas, Nuevo León, and San Luis Potosí in eastern México.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, Mexico
The Santo Domingo volcanic field lies in the center of the state of San Luis Potosí in the southern Basin and Range province of central México, ~50 km NE of the Ventura volcanic field.
Basin and Range Volcanic Province, Mexico
The Ventura Volcanic Field consists of a group of maars and pyroclastic cones located immediately NE of the city of San Luis Potosí in the southern Basin and Range province of central México.

Volcán San Juan, the NW-most major volcano of the Mexican Volcanic Belt, overlooks the city of Tepic, the capital of Nayarit state. The northernmost of two twin stratovolcanoes is truncated by a 1 x 4 km wide, oval-shaped caldera formed about 15,000 years ago during an eruption that produced thick rhyodacitic pumice-fa…

Volcán Las Navajas is a low-profile shield volcano located immediately north of the more prominent Sangangüey volcano. Las Navajas is truncated by a 4-km-wide circular caldera, associated with eruption of the Las Cuevas ash.

The scenic lake-filled Santa María del Oro maar lies between Sangangüey and Ceboruco volcanoes in the Tepic-Chapala graben. The topographically indistinct outer flanks of the maar give little hint to the dramatic 400 m drop into the Laguna Santa María crater lake.

Volcán Tepetiltic is an andesitic and dacitic stratovolcano truncated by an elliptical 5 x 2.5 km caldera that contains a lake at its NE corner. The caldera, with steep-sided walls elongated NE-SW, originated during a major rhyodacitic eruption that produced Plinian-airfall, pyroclastic-flow, and pyroclastic-surge depo…
The elliptical 7 x 10 km wide San Pedro caldera, located immediately south of the Tepetiltic caldera, is partially filled by the three coalescing Cerro San Pedro lava domes.

A mostly Pliocene volcanic field is located near the town of Los Volcanes, at the southern end of the Atenguillo graben in the Jalisco tectonic block of western México. The 285 km2 field consists of lava cones and flat-topped flows overlying Cretaceous ignimbrites.
